chapter_sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Elements can be classified as metals or non-metals based on their properties.
Metals are generally hard, lustrous, malleable, ductile, and good conductors.
Non-metals are neither malleable nor ductile; they are bad conductors of heat and electricity, except graphite.
Metals form positive ions by losing electrons to non-metals.
The reactivity of metals varies - potassium is most reactive, gold is least reactive.
Metals occur in nature as free elements or in the form of their compounds.
The extraction of metals from their ores and refining them is called metallurgy.
Corrosion is the deterioration of metals when exposed to moisture and air.

DEFINITION: Physical properties are characteristics of a substance that can be observed or measured without changing its chemical composition. Metals and non-metals differ significantly in their physical properties such as lustre, hardness, malleability, ductility, conductivity, and sonority.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Metals and non-metals are classified on the basis of their physical properties.
Most metals are solids at room temperature; mercury is an exception (liquid).
Iodine is a non-metal but it is lustrous.
Carbon (diamond) is the hardest natural substance; graphite (another form of carbon) conducts electricity.
Alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium) are so soft they can be cut with a knife.
Elements can exist in different forms called allotropes (e.g., diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon).

sections.label: ACTIVITY 3.1:
sections.aim: To observe the lustre of metal surfaces before and after cleaning.
sections.materials: Samples of iron, copper, aluminium and magnesium; sand paper.
procedure: - Take samples of iron, copper, aluminium and magnesium.
- Note the appearance of each sample.
- Clean the surface of each sample by rubbing with sand paper and note their appearance again.
sections.observation: After cleaning with sand paper, the surface of each metal shows a shining appearance.
sections.conclusion: Metals in their pure state have a shining surface called metallic lustre.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 3.2:
sections.aim: To test the hardness of metals.
sections.materials: Small pieces of iron, copper, aluminium, magnesium, and sodium metal.
procedure: - Try to cut the metals (iron, copper, aluminium, magnesium) with a sharp knife.
- Hold a piece of sodium metal with a pair of tongs (CAUTION: dry between filter paper folds).
- Put sodium on a watch-glass and try to cut it with a knife.
- Note observations.
sections.observation: Iron, copper, aluminium and magnesium are hard and cannot be easily cut. Sodium can be cut easily with a knife.
sections.conclusion: Metals are generally hard but hardness varies. Alkali metals like sodium are soft.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 3.3:
sections.aim: To test the malleability of metals.
sections.materials: Pieces of iron, zinc, lead and copper; block of iron; hammer.
procedure: - Take pieces of iron, zinc, lead and copper.
- Place any one metal on a block of iron and strike it four or five times with a hammer.
- Repeat with other metals.
- Record the change in shape of these metals.
sections.observation: The metals can be beaten into thin sheets without breaking.
sections.conclusion: Metals can be beaten into thin sheets. This property is called malleability. Gold and silver are the most malleable metals.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 3.4:
sections.aim: To identify metals that can be drawn into wires (ductility).
sections.materials: Various metal wires seen in daily life.
procedure: List the metals whose wires you have seen in daily life.
sections.observation: Copper, aluminium, iron and gold are commonly drawn into wires.
sections.conclusion: The ability of metals to be drawn into thin wires is called ductility. Gold is the most ductile metal - a wire of about 2 km can be drawn from one gram of gold.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 3.5:
sections.aim: To test the thermal conductivity of metals.
sections.materials: Aluminium or copper wire, stand, clamp, pin, wax, spirit lamp/candle.
procedure: - Take an aluminium or copper wire.
- Clamp this wire on a stand as shown in Fig. 3.1.
- Fix a pin to the free end of the wire using wax.
- Heat the wire with a spirit lamp, candle or burner near the place where it is clamped.
- Observe after some time. Note whether the metal wire melts.
sections.observation: The pin fixed with wax falls after some time of heating one end of the wire.
sections.conclusion: Metals are good conductors of heat and have high melting points. The best conductors of heat are silver and copper. Lead and mercury are comparatively poor conductors.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 3.6:
sections.aim: To test the electrical conductivity of metals.
sections.materials: Battery, bulb, switch, clips, connecting wires, metal samples.
procedure: - Set up an electric circuit as shown in Fig. 3.2.
- Place the metal to be tested in the circuit between terminals A and B.
- Observe whether the bulb glows.
sections.observation: The bulb glows when metals are placed in the circuit.
sections.conclusion: Metals are good conductors of electricity. This is why electric wires are made of metals like copper and aluminium.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 3.7:
sections.aim: To compare physical properties of non-metals with metals.
sections.materials: Samples of carbon (coal or graphite), sulphur and iodine.
procedure: - Collect samples of carbon (coal or graphite), sulphur and iodine.
- Carry out Activities 3.1 to 3.4 and 3.6 with these non-metals.
- Record your observations.
sections.observation: Non-metals do not show metallic lustre (except iodine), are not malleable, not ductile, and generally do not conduct electricity (except graphite).
sections.conclusion:
Non-metals have physical properties opposite to metals. Results compiled in Table 3.1.

items.question: What is metallic lustre? Give one example of a non-metal that shows lustre.
items.answer: Metallic lustre is the shining surface that metals have in their pure state. Example: Iodine is a non-metal that shows lustre.

items.question: Name the property by which metals can be beaten into thin sheets. Which are the most malleable metals?
items.answer: The property by which metals can be beaten into thin sheets is called malleability. Gold and silver are the most malleable metals.

items.question: Differentiate between malleability and ductility with examples.
items.answer:
- MALLEABILITY: The ability of metals to be beaten into thin sheets is called malleability. Example: Gold and silver are the most malleable metals. Aluminium foil used for wrapping food is an example of malleability.
- DUCTILITY: The ability of metals to be drawn into thin wires is called ductility. Example: Gold is the most ductile metal; a wire of about 2 km can be drawn from just one gram of gold.
- Malleability involves beating/rolling into sheets, whereas ductility involves drawing into wires.

items.question: State four physical properties of metals with one example for each property.
items.answer:
(i) LUSTRE: Metals have a shining surface in their pure state, called metallic lustre. Example: Copper has a reddish lustre.
(ii) MALLEABILITY: Metals can be beaten into thin sheets. Example: Gold is beaten into gold leaf.
(iii) DUCTILITY: Metals can be drawn into thin wires. Example: Copper is drawn into electrical wires.
(iv) CONDUCTIVITY: Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity. Example: Silver is the best conductor of heat and electricity.

items.question: State any four exceptions to the general physical properties of metals and non-metals.
items.answer:
(i) Mercury is a metal but it is a liquid at room temperature (exception: metals are solids).
(ii) Iodine is a non-metal but it has a lustrous surface (exception: non-metals are non-lustrous).
(iii) Carbon (diamond) is a non-metal but it has a very high melting point (exception: non-metals have low melting points).
(iv) Graphite is a non-metal but it is a good conductor of electricity (exception: non-metals are bad conductors).

items.question: Compare the physical properties of metals and non-metals under the following headings: (i) Physical state (ii) Lustre (iii) Malleability and ductility (iv) Conductivity (v) Melting and boiling points (vi) Sonority.
items.answer:
(i) PHYSICAL STATE: Most metals are solids at room temperature; exception - mercury is liquid. Non-metals are solids, liquids, or gases; bromine is the only liquid non-metal.
(ii) LUSTRE: Metals have shining metallic lustre in pure state. Non-metals are generally dull; exception - iodine is lustrous.
(iii) MALLEABILITY AND DUCTILITY: Metals are malleable (can be beaten into sheets) and ductile (can be drawn into wires). Non-metals are neither malleable nor ductile; they are brittle.
(iv) CONDUCTIVITY: Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity. Non-metals are bad conductors of heat and electricity; exception - graphite conducts electricity.
(v) MELTING AND BOILING POINTS: Metals generally have high melting and boiling points; exception - gallium and caesium have very low melting points. Non-metals generally have low melting and boiling points; exception - carbon (diamond) has very high melting point.
(vi) SONORITY: Metals produce a ringing sound when struck. Non-metals do not produce a ringing sound. School bells are made of metals because of their sonority.

items.question: Which property of metals allows them to be beaten into thin sheets?
items.explanation: Malleability is the property of metals to be beaten into thin sheets. Ductility is the property of being drawn into wires.

items.question: Which of the following metals is a liquid at room temperature?
items.explanation: Mercury is the only metal that exists as a liquid at room temperature. All other metals listed are solids at room temperature.

items.question: Which non-metal is a good conductor of electricity?
items.explanation: Graphite, an allotrope of carbon, is a good conductor of electricity. Sulphur, iodine, and phosphorus are all bad conductors.

items.question: Gold is the most ductile metal. Approximately what length of wire can be drawn from 1 gram of gold?
items.explanation: Gold is so ductile that about 2 km of wire can be drawn from just one gram of gold. This makes gold the most ductile of all metals.

items.question: Which of the following is an allotrope of carbon that is the hardest natural substance?
items.explanation: Diamond is an allotrope of carbon and is the hardest natural substance known, with a very high melting and boiling point. Graphite is another allotrope that is soft and conducts electricity.

items.question: Sodium and potassium are stored in kerosene oil because they:

options.B: React vigorously with air and water

items.explanation: Sodium and potassium (alkali metals) are so reactive that they catch fire if kept in open air. They react vigorously with both air and water. Kerosene oil prevents contact with air and moisture.

items.question: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes metals from non-metals?

options.A: All metals are solids while all non-metals are gases
options.B: All metals conduct electricity while no non-metal does
options.C: Metals form basic oxides while most non-metals form acidic oxides
options.D: Metals are malleable and ductile while non-metals are always brittle

items.explanation: Metals form basic oxides when burnt in air. Most non-metals form acidic oxides. Options A and B are incorrect because mercury is liquid and graphite conducts electricity. Option D is wrong because some non-metals like sulphur can be both forms.

items.question: A substance has metallic lustre, cannot be cut with a knife, and produces a ringing sound when struck but does not conduct electricity in any state. This substance is most likely a:
items.explanation: Iodine is a non-metal that has metallic lustre (lustre is normally a metal property). However, iodine does not conduct electricity, which is characteristic of non-metals. Options A and C would conduct electricity.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Metals have a shining surface called metallic lustre.
Most metals are hard; alkali metals (Na, K, Li) are soft and can be cut with a knife.
Malleability: ability to be beaten into thin sheets (gold and silver are most malleable).
Ductility: ability to be drawn into thin wires (gold is most ductile; 2 km wire from 1 g gold).
Metals are good conductors of heat; best conductors are silver and copper.
Metals are good conductors of electricity; used in making electric wires.
Metals produce a sound (sonorous) when struck; school bells made of metal.
Most metals have high melting and boiling points; exceptions: gallium and caesium have very low melting points.
Mercury is liquid at room temperature; only liquid metal.
Anodising: a process of forming a thick oxide layer on aluminium to make it resistant to corrosion; the oxide layer can be dyed to give attractive finish.

items.question: Define ductility. Name the most ductile metal.
items.answer: Ductility is the ability of metals to be drawn into thin wires. Gold is the most ductile metal; about 2 km of wire can be drawn from just 1 gram of gold.

items.question: What is anodising? Why is anodised aluminium more useful?
items.answer: Anodising is a process of forming a thick oxide layer on aluminium. When aluminium is exposed to air, it develops a thin oxide coat that makes it resistant to further corrosion. During anodising, a clean aluminium article is made the anode and electrolysed with dilute sulphuric acid. The oxygen gas evolved at the anode reacts with aluminium to form a thicker oxide layer. This oxide layer: (i) makes aluminium more resistant to corrosion, (ii) can be dyed easily to give an attractive finish, making anodised aluminium highly useful for cookware, window frames, and decorative items.

items.question: State the general physical properties of metals. Give one exception to each property.
items.answer:
(i) LUSTRE: Metals have a shining surface. Exception: metals like lead have a dull surface when exposed to air (they form an oxide coat).
(ii) HARDNESS: Metals are generally hard. Exception: alkali metals (sodium, potassium, lithium) are so soft they can be cut with a knife.
(iii) MALLEABILITY AND DUCTILITY: Metals are malleable and ductile. Exception: metals like zinc become brittle when cold.
(iv) CONDUCTIVITY: Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity. Exception: lead and mercury are comparatively poor conductors of heat.
(v) MELTING POINT: Metals generally have high melting points. Exception: gallium (melts on your palm) and caesium have very low melting points.

items.question: Which of the following metals can be cut with a knife?
items.explanation: Sodium is an alkali metal that is so soft it can be easily cut with a knife. Iron, copper, and aluminium are hard metals that cannot be cut with a knife.

items.question: What is the best conductor of heat among metals?
items.explanation: Silver is the best conductor of heat among all metals. Copper is the second best. Lead and mercury are poor conductors of heat.

items.question: Why are metals used in making bells?
items.explanation: Metals produce a ringing sound when struck; this property is called sonority. Because metals are sonorous, they are used in making bells, school bells, and musical instruments.

items.question: In the process of anodising aluminium, aluminium is made:
items.explanation: In anodising, a clean aluminium article is made the ANODE and electrolysed with dilute sulphuric acid. The oxygen evolved at the anode reacts with aluminium to form a thicker protective oxide layer.

items.question: Gallium is a metal that melts if kept on your palm. What can you conclude from this?

options.A: Gallium is not a true metal
options.B: Gallium has a very low melting point near body temperature
options.C: Gallium does not have metallic properties

items.explanation: Gallium has an unusually low melting point (~29.76 degree Celsius) which is close to human body temperature (37 degree Celsius). This is an exception to the general property that metals have high melting points. Gallium is still a true metal with metallic properties.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Non-metals can be solids, liquids, or gases: carbon, sulphur, iodine, phosphorus are solids; bromine is a liquid; oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen are gases.
Non-metals are generally dull (non-lustrous); exception: iodine is lustrous.
Non-metals are neither malleable nor ductile; they are brittle.
Non-metals are bad conductors of heat and electricity; exception: graphite conducts electricity.
Most non-metals have low melting and boiling points; exception: carbon (diamond) has very high melting point.
Non-metals do not produce a ringing sound when struck (not sonorous).
Carbon can exist in different forms called allotropes: diamond (hardest natural substance), graphite (conducts electricity), and charcoal.
TABLE 3.1 - Comparison of metals and non-metals:
PROPERTY        | METALS                        | NON-METALS
Type of surface | Shiny (lustrous)              | Dull (except iodine)
Hardness        | Generally hard (except Na, K) | Generally soft (except diamond)
Malleability    | Malleable                     | Non-malleable (brittle)
Ductility       | Ductile                       | Non-ductile
Conducts elect. | Yes (good conductors)         | No (except graphite)
Sonority        | Sonorous                      | Non-sonorous
State at RT     | Solid (except Hg)             | Solid, liquid or gas

items.question: Name any two exceptions to the general physical properties of non-metals.
items.answer:
(i) Iodine is a non-metal but it is lustrous (shiny surface).
(ii) Graphite is a non-metal but it is a good conductor of electricity.

items.question: What are allotropes? Name the allotropes of carbon and state one special property of each.
items.answer:
The different forms in which an element can exist are called allotropes. Carbon has three allotropes:
(i) DIAMOND: The hardest natural substance known. Has a very high melting and boiling point. Used in cutting tools and jewellery.
(ii) GRAPHITE: A good conductor of electricity. Used in making electrodes, pencils, and as a lubricant.
(iii) CHARCOAL/COAL: Used as a fuel. Can absorb gases and is used in filters.

items.question: State the general physical properties of non-metals and compare them with metals.
items.answer:
(i) PHYSICAL STATE: Non-metals can be solids (carbon, sulphur), liquids (bromine), or gases (oxygen, nitrogen). Metals are mostly solids; mercury is the only liquid metal.
(ii) LUSTRE: Non-metals are generally dull and non-lustrous. Metals are lustrous. Exception: iodine (non-metal) is lustrous.
(iii) MALLEABILITY/DUCTILITY: Non-metals are neither malleable nor ductile; they are brittle. Metals are malleable and ductile.
(iv) CONDUCTIVITY: Non-metals are bad conductors of heat and electricity. Metals are good conductors. Exception: graphite (non-metal) conducts electricity.
(v) MELTING POINT: Most non-metals have low melting points. Metals generally have high melting points. Exception: diamond (non-metal) has very high melting point.

items.question: Which of the following is a non-metal that exists as a liquid at room temperature?
items.explanation: Bromine is the only non-metal that exists as a liquid at room temperature. Iodine, sulphur, and phosphorus are solid non-metals.

items.question: Which allotrope of carbon is the hardest natural substance?
items.explanation: Diamond is an allotrope of carbon and is the hardest natural substance known. It has very high melting and boiling points. Graphite is another allotrope that is soft and conducts electricity.

items.question: Why is graphite considered an exception among non-metals?

options.B: It can be beaten into thin sheets
options.C: It is a good conductor of electricity

items.explanation: Graphite is an allotrope of carbon (a non-metal) but it is a good conductor of electricity. This is an exception because all other non-metals are bad conductors of electricity. Graphite is used in making electrodes.

items.question: Non-metals are described as brittle. This means they:
items.explanation: Brittle means the material breaks or shatters into pieces when force is applied. Non-metals are brittle because they lack malleability and ductility. This contrasts with metals that can be beaten or drawn without breaking.

items.question: Carbon is a non-metal. Why does diamond (an allotrope of carbon) not follow typical non-metal properties?

options.C: Diamond has an extremely high melting point, unlike typical non-metals
options.D: Diamond is a liquid at room temperature

items.explanation: Diamond has an extremely high melting point (about 3550 degree Celsius), unlike most non-metals which have low melting points. This makes diamond an exception to the general properties of non-metals. Diamond does not conduct electricity (typical non-metal behavior) and is not malleable.

DEFINITION: Chemical properties of metals refer to how metals react with other substances like oxygen, water, acids, and salt solutions. Different metals show different reactivities with these reagents.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Almost all metals combine with oxygen to form metal oxides: Metal + Oxygen -> Metal oxide
Metal oxides are basic in nature; some (like Al2O3 and ZnO) are amphoteric (react with both acids and bases).
Metals react with water to produce metal oxide and hydrogen gas: Metal + Water -> Metal oxide + Hydrogen
Metal oxides soluble in water form metal hydroxides (alkalis): Metal oxide + Water -> Metal hydroxide
Metals above hydrogen in the activity series can displace hydrogen from dilute acids.
HNO3 is an exception - hydrogen gas is not evolved with HNO3 (strong oxidising agent).
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution.
The reactivity series is a list of metals arranged in the order of decreasing reactivity.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 3.8:
sections.aim: To compare the chemical properties of metals and non-metals by burning in air.
sections.materials: Magnesium ribbon, sulphur powder, red and blue litmus paper, water.
procedure: - Burn a magnesium ribbon. Collect the ashes and dissolve in water.
- Test the solution with red and blue litmus paper.
- Burn sulphur powder and hold a test tube over the burning sulphur to collect fumes.
- Add water to the test tube and shake. Test with litmus paper.
sections.observation: Magnesium ash dissolved in water turns red litmus blue (basic). Sulphur fumes dissolved in water turns blue litmus red (acidic).
sections.conclusion:
Most metals produce basic oxides when burnt in air. Most non-metals produce acidic oxides.

items.question: Why is sodium stored in kerosene oil?
items.answer: Sodium is a highly reactive metal. It reacts vigorously with oxygen and moisture in air. If kept in open air, it can catch fire. It also reacts violently with water. To prevent accidental fires and protect it from reacting with air and moisture, sodium is stored immersed in kerosene oil.

items.question: Write the chemical equation for the reaction of iron with steam.
items.answer:
Iron does not react with cold or hot water but reacts with steam:
3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) -> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g)
Iron reacts with steam to form iron(II,III) oxide (Fe3O4) and hydrogen gas.

items.question: What happens when metals react with acids? Why does hydrogen gas not evolve when HNO3 reacts with a metal?
items.answer:
When metals react with dilute acids, they produce salt and hydrogen gas:
Metal + Dilute acid -> Salt + Hydrogen
For example: Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2
However, hydrogen gas is NOT evolved when HNO3 (nitric acid) reacts with metals (except magnesium and manganese). This is because HNO3 is a strong oxidising agent. It oxidises the H2 produced to water. Instead of H2, nitrogen oxides (N2O, NO, NO2) are evolved.

items.question: Explain the displacement reaction of metals with salt solutions. Give two examples with equations.
items.answer:
A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from its salt solution. This is called a displacement reaction:
Metal A + Salt solution of B -> Salt solution of A + Metal B (if A is more reactive than B)
Example 1: When zinc is added to copper sulphate solution, zinc displaces copper:
Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s)
(The blue colour of copper sulphate solution fades as colourless zinc sulphate forms and copper metal is deposited.)
Example 2: When iron is added to copper sulphate solution:
Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s)
(The blue colour fades and reddish copper deposits on iron nail.)

items.question: Describe the order of reactivity of metals with water. Give examples and equations.
items.answer:
(i) VERY REACTIVE (cold water): Potassium and sodium react violently with cold water.
2K(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2KOH(aq) + H2(g) + heat energy
2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g) + heat energy
(ii) LESS REACTIVE (hot water): Calcium reacts less vigorously with cold water. It floats due to bubbles of H2.
Ca(s) + 2H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq) + H2(g)
(iii) REACT WITH STEAM: Aluminium, iron and zinc react only with steam.
2Al(s) + 3H2O(g) -> Al2O3(s) + 3H2(g)
3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) -> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g)
(iv) DO NOT REACT: Metals like lead, copper, silver, and gold do not react with water at all.

items.question: Write notes on: (a) Metal oxides and their nature (b) Amphoteric oxides (c) Aqua regia.
items.answer:
(a) METAL OXIDES AND THEIR NATURE:
When metals are burnt in air, they combine with oxygen to form metal oxides:
Metal + Oxygen -> Metal oxide
Most metal oxides are basic in nature. Metal oxides that dissolve in water form alkalis (metal hydroxides):
Na2O(s) + H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq)
K2O(s) + H2O(l) -> 2KOH(aq)
2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO (Copper(II) oxide - black, basic)
4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3 (Aluminium oxide)

(b) AMPHOTERIC OXIDES:
Some metal oxides (like aluminium oxide and zinc oxide) show both acidic and basic behaviour. Such oxides are called amphoteric oxides. They react with both acids and bases:
Al2O3 + 6HCl -> 2AlCl3 + 3H2O (reacts with acid)
Al2O3 + 2NaOH -> 2NaAlO2 + H2O (reacts with base/sodium aluminate)

(c) AQUA REGIA:
Aqua regia (Latin for 'royal water') is a freshly prepared mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated nitric acid in the ratio of 3:1. It is a highly corrosive, fuming liquid. Aqua regia can dissolve gold and platinum, even though neither of these acids alone can do so. It is one of the few reagents able to dissolve gold and platinum.

items.question: What is the general equation for the reaction of a metal with water?
items.explanation: Metals react with water to produce metal oxide and hydrogen gas. Metal oxides that are soluble in water further react to form metal hydroxides.

items.question: Which metal reacts with cold water to produce hydrogen gas with a lot of heat?
items.explanation: Sodium reacts very vigorously with cold water, producing NaOH and H2 gas with a large amount of heat. The reaction is so exothermic that the evolved hydrogen catches fire.

items.question: What is the product when aluminium reacts with oxygen?
items.explanation: When aluminium reacts with oxygen: 4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3 (aluminium oxide). The formula is Al2O3 because aluminium has a valency of 3 and oxygen has a valency of 2.

items.question: The reactivity order of metals with water is: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al. Which of the following metals floats on water due to bubbles of hydrogen?
items.explanation: Calcium reacts less vigorously with water. Calcium starts floating due to bubbles of hydrogen gas sticking to its surface. Potassium and sodium react so vigorously that the hydrogen catches fire immediately.

items.question: Why does copper not produce hydrogen when added to dilute hydrochloric acid?

options.B: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series
options.D: Copper reacts with acid to form a gas other than hydrogen

items.explanation: Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series can displace hydrogen from dilute acids. Since copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, it cannot displace hydrogen and hence does not react with dilute HCl.

items.question: What is aqua regia? Which metals can it dissolve?

options.A: Pure HNO3; dissolves iron and zinc
options.B: Mixture of HCl and HNO3 (3:1); dissolves gold and platinum
options.C: Mixture of H2SO4 and HCl (1:3); dissolves silver

items.explanation: Aqua regia is a freshly prepared mixture of concentrated HCl and concentrated HNO3 in the ratio 3:1. It can dissolve gold and platinum - metals that cannot be dissolved by either acid alone.

items.question: Zinc oxide reacts with both NaOH and HCl. What type of oxide is it?
items.explanation: An oxide that reacts with both acids and bases to form salt and water is called an amphoteric oxide. Zinc oxide and aluminium oxide are examples. They are neither purely basic nor purely acidic.

items.question: Four metals A, B, C and D were tested with water, dilute HCl, and salt solutions. Metal A reacts with cold water, B reacts only with hot water, C reacts only with steam, D does not react with water or acid. The correct order of reactivity is:
items.explanation: The reactivity decreases as the ability to react with water decreases. A reacts with cold water (most reactive), B with hot water, C only with steam (less reactive), and D not at all (least reactive). So A > B > C > D.

subtopics.subtopic_name: WHAT HAPPENS WHEN METALS ARE BURNT IN AIR?

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Almost all metals combine with oxygen to form metal oxides:
Metal + Oxygen -> Metal oxide
Example: 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO (Copper forms black copper(II) oxide)
Example: 4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3 (Aluminium forms aluminium oxide)
Most metal oxides are basic in nature.
Some metal oxides are AMPHOTERIC: react with both acids AND bases.
Aluminium oxide (Al2O3) and zinc oxide (ZnO) are amphoteric oxides.
Al2O3 + 6HCl -> 2AlCl3 + 3H2O (reacts with acid)
Al2O3 + 2NaOH -> 2NaAlO2 + H2O (reacts with base)
Metal oxides soluble in water form alkalis:
Na2O(s) + H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq)
K2O(s) + H2O(l) -> 2KOH(aq)

Reactivity differences: K, Na, Ca react vigorously (catch fire); Mg burns vigorously; Al, Zn form thin protective oxide layers; Fe burns as filings; Cu does not burn but forms black CuO; Ag, Au do not react with oxygen.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 3.9:
sections.aim: To study the reaction of different metals with oxygen in air and arrange them in order of reactivity.
sections.materials: Metal samples of Al, Cu, Fe, Pb, Mg, Zn, Na; tongs; flame.
procedure: - CAUTION: Needs teacher's assistance; students should wear eye protection.
- Hold any of the samples taken above with a pair of tongs and try burning over a flame.
- Repeat with other metal samples.
- Collect the product if formed.
- Let the products and the metal surface cool down.

- Observe: Which metals burn easily? What flame colour is observed? How does the metal surface appear after burning? Arrange the metals in decreasing order of reactivity towards oxygen. Are the products soluble in water?
sections.observation: Sodium catches fire vigorously. Magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame. Aluminium and zinc form thin oxide layers. Iron filings burn vigorously in the flame (not the solid metal). Copper becomes coated with black CuO. Silver and gold do not react.
sections.conclusion:
Different metals show different reactivities towards oxygen. Sodium is the most reactive and silver/gold are the least reactive.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: What are amphoteric oxides? Give two examples.
items.answer:
Amphoteric oxides are metal oxides that react with both acids and bases to form salt and water. They show both acidic and basic properties.
Examples: Aluminium oxide (Al2O3) and zinc oxide (ZnO).

items.question: Write the equation for the reaction of sodium oxide with water.
items.answer:
Sodium oxide reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide (an alkali):
Na2O(s) + H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq)
Similarly: K2O(s) + H2O(l) -> 2KOH(aq)

items.question: Write equations showing that aluminium oxide is amphoteric.
items.answer:
Aluminium oxide (Al2O3) is amphoteric because it reacts with both acids and bases:
With acid: Al2O3 + 6HCl -> 2AlCl3 + 3H2O
With base: Al2O3 + 2NaOH -> 2NaAlO2 + H2O (sodium aluminate)
This shows that Al2O3 behaves as a basic oxide with acids and as an acidic oxide with bases, hence it is amphoteric.

items.question: Explain how different metals react with oxygen by giving the reactivity order. Give equations for two examples.
items.answer:
Almost all metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides. The reactivity differs:
MOST REACTIVE: K and Na react so vigorously that they catch fire in open air.
MODERATELY REACTIVE: Mg burns with dazzling white flame. Al, Zn, Pb develop a thin oxide protective layer at ordinary temperature.
LESS REACTIVE: Iron (Fe) does not burn on heating but iron filings burn vigorously when sprinkled in the flame of a burner.
LEAST REACTIVE: Copper forms black CuO when heated but does not burn. Silver and gold do not react with oxygen even at high temperatures.
Equations:
2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO (Copper(II) oxide - black)
4Al + 3O2 -> 2Al2O3 (Aluminium oxide)

items.question: Why do different metals have different tendencies to form oxides? What is the significance of a protective oxide layer?
items.answer:
Different metals react with oxygen at different rates due to their different positions in the reactivity series. Metals at the top of the reactivity series (K, Na, Ca) have a stronger tendency to lose electrons and hence react vigorously with oxygen. Metals at the bottom (Ag, Au, Pt) have little tendency to lose electrons and do not react with oxygen.
SIGNIFICANCE OF PROTECTIVE OXIDE LAYER: Some metals like aluminium, zinc, and magnesium form thin but very dense oxide layers on their surface when exposed to air. This oxide layer acts as a protective coating and prevents the underlying metal from further oxidation or corrosion. For example:
- Aluminium develops Al2O3 layer that makes it resistant to corrosion.
- This is why aluminium utensils and window frames do not rust despite exposure to air.
- Anodising artificially increases the thickness of this oxide layer on aluminium.

items.question: Compare the reactions of three metals (Na, Mg, Cu) with oxygen and state their equations, observations, and nature of the products formed.
items.answer:
SODIUM (Na):
Reaction: 4Na + O2 -> 2Na2O (sodium oxide)
Observation: Sodium catches fire if kept in open air; reacts so vigorously it can cause an explosion.
Nature of product: Na2O is a basic oxide; dissolves in water to form NaOH (alkali):
Na2O + H2O -> 2NaOH

MAGNESIUM (Mg):
Reaction: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO (magnesium oxide)
Observation: Magnesium burns in air with a dazzling white flame.
Nature of product: MgO is a basic oxide; dissolves slightly in water to form Mg(OH)2. Magnesium ash dissolved in water turns red litmus blue.

COPPER (Cu):
Reaction: 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO (copper(II) oxide)
Observation: Copper does not burn. When heated, the hot copper surface becomes coated with black CuO. At very high temperatures, copper does not react.
Nature of product: CuO is a basic oxide; does not dissolve in water but reacts with acids. Silver and gold do not react with oxygen at all.

items.question: What colour change occurs when magnesium is burnt in air?

options.B: Magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame

items.explanation: Magnesium burns in air with a characteristic dazzling white flame, producing white magnesium oxide (MgO). This is a commonly used identification test for magnesium.

items.question: Which of the following metal oxides is amphoteric?
items.explanation: Al2O3 (aluminium oxide) is an amphoteric oxide - it reacts with both acids and bases. Na2O, CuO, and Fe2O3 are basic oxides only.

items.question: What is the black coating formed on the surface of copper when heated in air?
items.explanation: When copper is heated in air, it reacts with oxygen to form a black coating of copper(II) oxide (CuO): 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO. This is a basic oxide.

items.question: Which of these metals does NOT react with oxygen even at high temperatures?
items.explanation: Silver and gold do not react with oxygen even at high temperatures. They are at the bottom of the reactivity series and are least reactive. Iron forms Fe3O4, copper forms CuO, aluminium forms Al2O3.

items.question: Aluminium is a very reactive metal yet it is used for making cooking vessels. Why?

options.A: Aluminium has a very high melting point
options.B: Aluminium forms a thin but dense protective Al2O3 layer that prevents further corrosion
options.D: Aluminium does not react with acid

items.explanation: Although aluminium is reactive, when exposed to air it quickly forms a thin, dense, and adherent layer of Al2O3 (aluminium oxide). This oxide layer is very stable and protects the underlying metal from further reaction with air, water, or acids. This protective layer makes aluminium suitable for cookware despite being reactive.

subtopics.subtopic_name: WHAT HAPPENS WHEN METALS REACT WITH WATER?

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: General equation: Metal + Water -> Metal oxide + Hydrogen
Metal oxide + Water -> Metal hydroxide
ORDER OF REACTIVITY WITH WATER:
1. K, Na: React violently with cold water; hydrogen gas catches fire:
2K(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2KOH(aq) + H2(g) + heat energy
2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g) + heat energy
2. Ca: Reacts less vigorously with cold water; floats due to H2 bubbles:
Ca(s) + 2H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq) + H2(g)
3. Mg: Does not react with cold water; reacts slowly with hot water.
4. Al, Zn, Fe: Do not react with cold or hot water; react with steam:
5. Pb, Cu, Ag, Au: Do not react with water at all.
Metal oxides soluble in water form alkalis.
Metals react with water to produce a metal oxide and hydrogen. Metals like lead, copper, silver and gold do not react with water.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 3.10:
sections.aim: To study reactions of different metals with water and arrange them in order of reactivity.
sections.materials: Samples of metals as in Activity 3.9; beakers; cold water; hot water; apparatus for steam (Fig. 3.3).
procedure: - CAUTION: Needs teacher's assistance.
- Collect the same metal samples as in Activity 3.9.
- Put small pieces of the samples separately in beakers half-filled with cold water.
- Observe: Which metals reacted with cold water? Arrange them in increasing order of reactivity with cold water.
- Did any metal produce fire on water?
- Does any metal start floating after some time?
- Put metals that did not react with cold water in beakers half-filled with hot water.
- For metals that did not react with hot water, arrange apparatus as shown in Fig. 3.3 and observe their reaction with steam.
- Which metals did not react even with steam?
- Arrange all metals in decreasing order of reactivity with water.
sections.observation: K and Na react violently with cold water (H2 catches fire). Ca reacts, floats on water. Mg reacts slowly with hot water. Al, Zn, Fe react with steam. Cu, Ag, Au do not react.
sections.conclusion:
Reactivity of metals with water decreases in the order: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > Cu > Ag > Au.

items.question: Why does calcium float on water when it reacts?
items.answer:
When calcium reacts with water, hydrogen gas is produced:
Ca(s) + 2H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq) + H2(g)
The bubbles of hydrogen gas produced stick to the surface of calcium, making it less dense than water. This causes calcium to float on the water surface.

items.question: Compare the reactions of potassium, calcium, and iron with water.
items.answer:
POTASSIUM: Reacts very violently with cold water. The reaction is so exothermic that the evolved hydrogen immediately catches fire.
2K(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2KOH(aq) + H2(g) + heat energy
CALCIUM: Reacts less violently with cold water. The reaction is not vigorous enough for hydrogen to catch fire. Calcium floats due to H2 bubbles sticking to its surface.
Ca(s) + 2H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq) + H2(g)
IRON: Does not react with cold or hot water. Reacts only with steam to form iron(II,III) oxide:
3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) -> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g)

items.question: Explain why some metals react with water vigorously while others do not react at all.
items.answer:
The reactivity of metals with water depends on their position in the reactivity series. The reactivity series lists metals in decreasing order of their chemical reactivity:
HIGHLY REACTIVE METALS (K, Na): These metals are at the top of the reactivity series. They have a very strong tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions. They react violently with cold water, producing heat so intense that the H2 gas evolved immediately catches fire.
MODERATELY REACTIVE (Ca, Mg): Calcium reacts with cold water but less vigorously. Magnesium does not react with cold water but reacts slowly with hot water.
LESS REACTIVE (Al, Zn, Fe): These metals react only with steam (high temperature water vapour). They do not react with cold or hot water because their oxide layers protect them.
LEAST REACTIVE (Cu, Ag, Au, Pb): These metals do not react with water at all. They are at the bottom of the reactivity series and have little tendency to lose electrons. They are found in nature in the free (uncombined) state.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Potassium reacts with water to form:
items.explanation: 2K(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2KOH(aq) + H2(g) + heat. Potassium reacts with water to form potassium hydroxide (KOH) and hydrogen gas. The reaction is highly exothermic.

items.question: Which of the following metals reacts with steam but not with cold or hot water?
items.explanation: Iron does not react with cold or hot water but reacts with steam: 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) -> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g). Sodium reacts with cold water, calcium reacts with cold water, gold does not react with water at all.

items.question: The equation 2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g) + heat shows that:

options.A: Sodium produces oxygen when reacting with water
options.C: The reaction is exothermic and produces hydrogen gas
options.D: Sodium does not react with cold water

items.explanation: The equation shows that sodium reacts with water to produce NaOH and H2 gas, with the release of heat energy. This confirms it is an exothermic reaction. NaOH is alkaline (basic), not acidic.

items.question: What product is formed when iron reacts with steam?
items.explanation: 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) -> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g). Iron reacts with steam to form Fe3O4 (iron(II,III) oxide, also called magnetite), not simple FeO or Fe2O3.

items.question: Magnesium does not react with cold water but reacts slowly with hot water. However, it reacts vigorously with steam. What does this tell about the nature of magnesium?

options.B: The reactivity of magnesium depends on the temperature of water
options.C: Magnesium is less reactive than iron
options.D: Magnesium does not react with water in any form

items.explanation: This shows that the reactivity of magnesium with water increases with temperature. At low temperature (cold water), Mg barely reacts. With hot water, it reacts slowly. With steam (very high temperature), it reacts vigorously. This is because higher temperatures provide more activation energy for the reaction.

subtopics.subtopic_name: WHAT HAPPENS WHEN METALS REACT WITH ACIDS?

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: General equation: Metal + Dilute acid -> Salt + Hydrogen
Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2 (most vigorous at room temperature)
Al + 2HCl: tarnished/oxide covered Al reacts slowly; need to remove oxide layer first.
Zn, Al, Fe react with dilute HCl.
Cu, Ag, Au: below hydrogen in reactivity series; do NOT react with dilute HCl.
Reactivity order with dilute HCl: Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu (Cu does not react).
EXCEPTION - NITRIC ACID (HNO3): H2 gas is not evolved when metals react with HNO3.
HNO3 is a strong oxidising agent; it oxidises the H2 produced to water.
Instead, nitrogen oxides (N2O, NO, NO2) are evolved.
Exception: Mg and Mn react with very dilute HNO3 to evolve H2.
Temperature of the reaction increases in the order: Mg reaction is most exothermic.
Rate of bubble formation (H2): Mg > Al > Zn > Fe (Cu = no bubbles).

sections.label: ACTIVITY 3.11:
sections.aim: To study the reactions of metals with dilute hydrochloric acid and compare their reactivity.
sections.materials: Metal samples (all except Na and K); dilute HCl; test tubes; thermometers.
procedure: - Collect all the metal samples except sodium and potassium (they react too vigorously with water).
- If the samples are tarnished, rub them clean with sand paper.
- Put the samples separately in test tubes containing dilute hydrochloric acid.
- Suspend thermometers in the test tubes so that their bulbs are dipped in the acid.
- Observe the rate of formation of bubbles carefully.
- Which metals reacted vigorously with dilute hydrochloric acid?
- With which metal did you record the highest temperature?
- Arrange the metals in the decreasing order of reactivity with dilute acids.
sections.observation: Mg reacts very vigorously (fastest bubbles, highest temperature). Al, Zn, Fe react at decreasing rates. Cu shows no reaction - no bubbles, temperature unchanged.
sections.conclusion:
Reactivity decreases: Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu. Copper does not react with dilute HCl.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Why does hydrogen gas not evolve when nitric acid reacts with most metals?
items.answer: HNO3 is a strong oxidising agent. When a metal reacts with HNO3, hydrogen gas is produced but HNO3 immediately oxidises it to water (H2O). Instead of H2, nitrogen oxides (N2O, NO, NO2) are produced. Exceptions: magnesium (Mg) and manganese (Mn) react with very dilute HNO3 to evolve H2.

items.question: Which of the following pairs will give displacement reaction and why?
items.answer:
(a) Iron and copper sulphate solution: YES, displacement reaction occurs.
Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s)
Iron is more reactive than copper (Fe is above Cu in the reactivity series). Hence, iron displaces copper from copper sulphate solution. The blue colour of copper sulphate solution fades and reddish-brown copper deposits on the iron.
(b) Copper and iron sulphate solution: NO displacement reaction.
Copper cannot displace iron from iron sulphate solution because copper is less reactive than iron (Cu is below Fe in the reactivity series). A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive metal from its solution.

items.question: Explain why copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid, but iron and zinc do. Write equations for iron and zinc reactions.
items.answer:
The reactivity series places metals in decreasing order of reactivity. Only metals ABOVE hydrogen in the reactivity series can displace hydrogen from dilute acids.
IRON (Fe): Iron is above hydrogen in the reactivity series. Hence it can displace hydrogen from dilute acids:
Fe(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> FeCl2(aq) + H2(g)
Iron + Dilute hydrochloric acid -> Iron(II) chloride + Hydrogen
ZINC (Zn): Zinc is above hydrogen. Similarly:
Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> ZnCl2(aq) + H2(g)
COPPER (Cu): Copper is BELOW hydrogen in the reactivity series. Therefore, copper cannot displace hydrogen from dilute acids. Adding copper to dilute HCl - no reaction occurs, no bubbles are formed, temperature remains unchanged. This is why copper is used in plumbing (doesn't react with dilute acids in water).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Which metal reacts most vigorously with dilute hydrochloric acid?
items.explanation: Magnesium (Mg) reacts most vigorously with dilute HCl, producing the most bubbles and the highest temperature. Reactivity order: Mg > Zn > Fe. Copper does not react at all with dilute HCl.

items.question: What gas is produced when zinc reacts with dilute sulphuric acid?
items.explanation: Zn(s) + H2SO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + H2(g). When zinc reacts with dilute sulphuric acid, zinc sulphate and hydrogen gas are produced. Hydrogen gas can be tested with a burning splint (it burns with a pop sound).

items.question: Magnesium and manganese react with very dilute HNO3 to produce hydrogen gas. What does this tell us?

options.A: HNO3 is not an oxidising agent with these metals
options.B: Mg and Mn are less reactive than other metals
options.C: HNO3 behaves differently with highly reactive metals Mg and Mn
options.D: H2 is always produced when metals react with HNO3

items.explanation: HNO3 is generally a strong oxidising agent and does not produce H2 with most metals. However, Mg and Mn are exceptions - they react with very dilute HNO3 to produce H2. This shows that with highly reactive metals and very dilute acid, normal acid-metal reaction can occur.

items.question: Why are tarnished metal samples rubbed with sandpaper before the Activity 3.11 experiment?

options.B: To remove the protective oxide layer so the metal can react with acid
options.C: To increase the size of the metal
options.D: To make the metal shiny for observation

items.explanation: When metals are exposed to air, they develop a layer of oxide on the surface (tarnishing). This oxide layer prevents the metal from coming in direct contact with the acid. Rubbing with sandpaper removes this layer so that the fresh metal surface can react with the dilute acid.

items.question: When iron is added to copper sulphate solution, the blue colour of the solution disappears. The correct explanation is:

options.A: Iron is dissolved by the copper sulphate solution
options.B: Iron displaces copper from solution as Fe is more reactive than Cu
options.C: Copper displaces iron as Cu is less reactive
options.D: Both iron and copper dissolve in the solution

items.explanation: Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s). Iron is more reactive than copper (Fe is above Cu in reactivity series). Iron displaces copper from the solution. The blue colour of CuSO4 disappears as colourless FeSO4 forms. Reddish copper deposits on the iron nail.

subtopics.subtopic_name: HOW DO METALS REACT WITH SOLUTIONS OF OTHER METAL SALTS?

sections.label: DEFINITION: A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from its salt solution. This is called a displacement reaction. The general equation is:
sections.text: Metal A + Salt solution of B -> Salt solution of A + Metal B (only if A is more reactive than B)

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Metal A + Salt solution of B -> Salt solution of A + Metal B (only if A is more reactive than B)
Example: Cu + 2AgNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag (copper displaces silver)
Example: Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu (zinc displaces copper)
Example: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu (iron displaces copper)
If Metal A is LESS reactive than Metal B, NO displacement occurs.
Example: Cu + FeSO4 -> No reaction (copper cannot displace iron)
Evidence of displacement reaction: colour change in solution, new metal deposited.
This principle helps determine the relative reactivity of metals (reactivity series).

sections.label: ACTIVITY 3.12:
sections.aim: To study the displacement reaction between metals and salt solutions, and compare reactivity.
sections.materials: Clean copper wire, iron nail, copper sulphate solution, iron sulphate solution, test tubes.
procedure: - Take a clean wire of copper and an iron nail.
- Put the copper wire in a solution of iron sulphate and the iron nail in a solution of copper sulphate taken in test tubes (Fig. 3.4).
- Record observations after 20 minutes.
- In which test tube did a reaction occur?
- On what basis can you say that a reaction has actually taken place?
- Can you correlate observations from Activities 3.9, 3.10 and 3.11?
- Write a balanced chemical equation for the reaction that has taken place.
- Name the type of reaction.
sections.observation: The iron nail in copper sulphate solution becomes coated with reddish copper. The blue colour of copper sulphate fades. No change occurs in the test tube with copper wire in iron sulphate solution.
sections.conclusion:
Iron is more reactive than copper. Iron displaces copper from copper sulphate solution:
Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s)
Copper cannot displace iron from iron sulphate solution (no reaction).
This is a single displacement reaction.

items.question: What is a displacement reaction? Give one example with equation.
items.answer:
A displacement reaction is a reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound (salt solution or other). Example:
Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s)
Iron is more reactive than copper, so iron displaces copper from copper sulphate solution. The blue colour of the solution fades as colourless FeSO4 is formed and reddish copper deposits.

items.question: From Activity 3.12, which metal (copper or iron) is more reactive? How did you determine this?
items.answer:
Iron is more reactive than copper. This was determined from Activity 3.12:
(i) When an iron nail was placed in copper sulphate (CuSO4) solution:
- The blue colour of the solution gradually faded.
- A reddish-brown coating appeared on the iron nail (copper deposited).
This shows: Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s)
(ii) When a copper wire was placed in iron sulphate (FeSO4) solution:
- No colour change occurred.
- No deposit was observed on the copper wire.
This means copper CANNOT displace iron from its solution, confirming iron is more reactive than copper.

items.question: Samples of four metals A, B, C and D were added to the following solutions one by one. The results obtained have been tabulated:
items.answer:
Analysis:
- Metal D: Cannot displace any metal; least reactive.
- Metal C: Can only displace silver (least reactive metal from options); C is more reactive than Ag but less than others.
- Metal A: Displaces copper but not iron or zinc; A is less reactive than Fe and Zn but more reactive than Cu.
- Metal B: Displaces Fe, Cu, Ag but not Zn; B is between Zn and Ag in reactivity.
Wait - B displaces Fe but not Zn, so B is more reactive than Fe but less than Zn.
Corrected order: B > A (B displaces Fe, A doesn't) -> Actually B > Zn position... Let us re-read: B does not displace Zn but displaces Fe.
Order: B > Fe level > A > Cu level > C > Ag level > D.
Decreasing reactivity: B > A > C > D.
(B is most reactive as it displaces iron, copper and silver; A displaces only copper; C displaces only silver; D displaces nothing.)

items.question: What change occurs when an iron nail is placed in copper sulphate solution?

options.A: The solution turns colourless and iron dissolves
options.B: Blue colour fades and reddish copper deposits on iron
options.C: Iron becomes shinier in the solution

items.explanation: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. Iron displaces copper from the solution. The blue colour of CuSO4 fades as colourless FeSO4 forms. Reddish copper metal gets deposited on the iron nail.

items.question: Which statement correctly describes a displacement reaction?

options.A: A less reactive metal displaces a more reactive metal from solution
options.B: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from solution
options.C: Two metals react with each other in the solid state
options.D: A metal reacts with acid to form hydrogen gas

items.explanation: In a displacement reaction, a more reactive metal displaces (pushes out) a less reactive metal from its salt solution. The reactivity series is used to predict which metal will displace the other.

items.question: Zinc is added to a solution of copper sulphate. Which observation is correct?

options.A: Zinc displaces copper; blue colour of solution fades
options.B: Copper displaces zinc; solution turns colourless
options.C: No reaction as zinc and copper are equally reactive
options.D: Zinc sulphate is converted to copper sulphate

items.explanation: Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s). Zinc is more reactive than copper. Zinc displaces copper from the blue copper sulphate solution, forming colourless zinc sulphate. The blue colour fades and copper deposits.

items.question: Which of the following will NOT show a displacement reaction?

options.A: Zinc added to copper sulphate solution
options.B: Iron added to silver nitrate solution
options.C: Copper added to zinc sulphate solution
options.D: Magnesium added to iron sulphate solution

items.explanation: Copper is less reactive than zinc (Cu is below Zn in reactivity series). Therefore, copper cannot displace zinc from zinc sulphate solution. All other options show displacement because the added metal is more reactive than the metal in solution.

items.question: In Activity 3.12, why was it important to have a clean copper wire (not tarnished)?

options.A: Tarnished copper is lighter than clean copper
options.B: The tarnish (oxide layer) on copper would react with iron sulphate
options.C: Tarnish prevents direct contact between the metal and solution, which may give misleading results
options.D: Clean copper is more reactive than tarnished copper

items.explanation: If the copper wire has an oxide layer (tarnish) on its surface, this layer prevents the metal from making proper contact with the solution. This may interfere with observations. Using a clean wire ensures that the fresh metal surface is in contact with the solution, giving accurate results about reactivity.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Metals are listed in decreasing order of reactivity: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.
Hydrogen (H) is included in the series though not a metal (as reference point for acids).
Metals above hydrogen in the series can displace hydrogen from dilute acids.
Metals above hydrogen in the series react with dilute acids to produce hydrogen gas.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution.
The reactivity series was developed after performing displacement experiments with metals and their salt solutions (Activities 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.12).
Potassium (K) is the most reactive metal; Gold (Au) is the least reactive.
Metals at the top (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) are obtained by electrolysis (high reactivity, cannot be reduced by carbon).
Metals in the middle (Zn, Fe, Pb) can be reduced using carbon (coke).
Metals at the bottom (Cu, Hg, Ag, Au) are found in free state in nature.

Na - Sodium
Ca - Calcium
Mg - Magnesium

Zn - Zinc        - Reactivity decreases
Fe - Iron
Pb - Lead
[H] - [Hydrogen]
Cu - Copper
Hg - Mercury
Ag - Silver

items.question: What is the reactivity series? Name the most reactive and least reactive metals.
items.answer:
The reactivity series is a list of metals arranged in the order of their decreasing chemical reactivity. It is based on the observations of reactions of metals with oxygen, water, dilute acids, and salt solutions.
Most reactive metal: Potassium (K).
Least reactive metal: Gold (Au).

items.question: Why is hydrogen included in the reactivity series even though it is not a metal?
items.answer:
Hydrogen is included in the reactivity series as a reference point even though it is not a metal, because:
(i) It helps us determine whether a metal can react with dilute acids: metals above hydrogen in the series can displace H2 from dilute acids, while metals below hydrogen cannot.
(ii) It provides a dividing line between reactive metals (above H) and less reactive metals (below H) with respect to acid reactions.
(iii) It connects metal reactivity to hydrogen evolution, which is an observable and measurable outcome.
For example: Fe (above H) reacts with HCl to give H2, but Cu (below H) does not react with HCl.

items.question: How was the reactivity series developed? Explain with the help of displacement reactions.
items.answer:
The reactivity series was developed through a series of systematic displacement experiments:
Step 1 - REACTIONS WITH OXYGEN: Metals were ranked by their reactivity with oxygen (Activity 3.9). K and Na reacted most vigorously, while Cu and Au did not react.
Step 2 - REACTIONS WITH WATER: Metals were tested with cold water, hot water, and steam (Activity 3.10). K and Na reacted with cold water; Fe only with steam; Cu not at all.
Step 3 - REACTIONS WITH DILUTE ACIDS: Metals were tested with dilute HCl (Activity 3.11). Mg reacted fastest, Cu did not react.
Step 4 - DISPLACEMENT REACTIONS: Metals were tested against salt solutions (Activity 3.12). A metal that displaced another from its solution was placed higher.
For example:
- Fe displaces Cu from CuSO4: Fe is more reactive than Cu.
- Zn displaces Fe from FeSO4: Zn is more reactive than Fe.
By combining all these observations, the complete reactivity series K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au was established.

items.question: Which metal is at the top of the reactivity series?
items.explanation: Potassium (K) is the most reactive metal and is at the top of the reactivity series. The order at the top is K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al.

items.question: Metals below hydrogen in the reactivity series:

options.B: Cannot displace hydrogen from dilute acids
options.C: Are more reactive than metals above hydrogen
options.D: React with water to produce hydrogen

items.explanation: Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series can displace hydrogen from dilute acids. Metals below hydrogen (Cu, Hg, Ag, Au) cannot react with dilute acids to produce hydrogen gas.

items.question: Which pair of metals would show a displacement reaction?
items.explanation: Zinc is above iron in the reactivity series. Therefore, zinc can displace iron from iron sulphate solution: Zn + FeSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Fe. Options A and B would not work as Cu < Zn and Ag < Cu. Option C would not work as Zn < Mg.

items.question: In an experiment, metal A displaces metal B from its salt solution. Metal B displaces metal C from its salt solution but C cannot displace A. What is the correct order of reactivity?
items.explanation: Since A displaces B, A is more reactive than B (A > B). Since B displaces C, B is more reactive than C (B > C). Therefore, the order is A > B > C.

items.question: Gold is found in nature as a free element while iron is found combined with oxygen. What does this tell about the reactivity of these metals?

options.A: Gold is more reactive than iron
options.B: Iron is less reactive than gold
options.C: Gold is least reactive; iron is reactive enough to form compounds
options.D: Iron and gold have equal reactivity

items.explanation: Metals at the bottom of the reactivity series (like gold, silver, platinum) are least reactive and are found in nature in the free (uncombined) state. Iron is moderately reactive and combines with oxygen to form iron oxide ores. The more reactive a metal, the stronger its compounds and the more difficult it is to extract the pure metal.

topics.topic_name: HOW DO METALS AND NON-METALS REACT?

sections.label: LIST OF SUB-TOPICS:
items: 3.3.1 Properties of Ionic Compounds

DEFINITION: Metals react with non-metals by transferring electrons from the metal to the non-metal. This electron transfer leads to the formation of ions, and the resulting compounds are called ionic compounds or electrovalent compounds.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Metals achieve stability by losing electrons (forming positive ions / cations).
Non-metals achieve stability by gaining electrons (forming negative ions / anions).
The electron lost by a metal is gained by a non-metal.
Example: Na (2,8,1) loses 1 electron -> Na+ (2,8)
Example: Cl (2,8,7) gains 1 electron -> Cl- (2,8,8)
Na+ and Cl- attract each other by electrostatic force to form NaCl (sodium chloride).
Mg (2,8,2) loses 2 electrons -> Mg2+ (2,8)
Each Cl- (2,8,8) gains 1 electron; so 2 Cl- ions needed -> MgCl2.
NaCl does not exist as molecules but as aggregates of oppositely charged ions.
Noble gases have completely filled valence shells, hence show little chemical activity.
Elements react to attain completely filled valence shells (like noble gases).
TABLE 3.3 - ELECTRONIC CONFIGURATIONS:
TYPE          | ELEMENT         | ATOMIC NO. | K | L | M | N
Noble gases   | Helium (He)     | 2          | 2 |   |   |
Metals        | Sodium (Na)     | 11         | 2 | 8 | 1 |
| Magnesium (Mg)  | 12         | 2 | 8 | 2 |
| Aluminium (Al)  | 13         | 2 | 8 | 3 |
| Potassium (K)   | 19         | 2 | 8 | 8 | 1
Non-metals    | Nitrogen (N)    | 7          | 2 | 5 |   |
| Fluorine (F)    | 9          | 2 | 7 |   |
| Phosphorus (P)  | 15         | 2 | 8 | 5 |
| Chlorine (Cl)   | 17         | 2 | 8 | 7 |
FORMATION OF NaCl (Fig. 3.5):
Na -> Na+ + e-   (2,8,1 -> 2,8 - sodium cation)
Cl + e- -> Cl-   (2,8,7 -> 2,8,8 - chloride anion)
Na+ + Cl- -> NaCl (held by electrostatic attraction)
FORMATION OF MgCl2 (Fig. 3.6):
Mg -> Mg2+ + 2e-  (2,8,2 -> 2,8 - magnesium cation)
Mg2+ + 2Cl- -> MgCl2
QUESTIONS (in-text, after Topic 3.3):
1. (i) Write the electron-dot structures for sodium, oxygen and magnesium.
(ii) Show the formation of Na2O and MgO by the transfer of electrons.
(iii) What are the ions present in these compounds?
2. Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?

items.question: What are ionic compounds? Give two examples.
items.answer:
Ionic compounds (also called electrovalent compounds) are compounds formed by the transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal. In this process, the metal forms a positively charged ion (cation) and the non-metal forms a negatively charged ion (anion). These opposite ions are held together by strong electrostatic forces.
Examples: Sodium chloride (NaCl), Magnesium chloride (MgCl2).

items.question: Write the electron-dot structure showing the formation of MgO by the transfer of electrons.
items.answer:
Formation of MgO (Magnesium oxide):
Mg (2,8,2) -> Mg2+ (2,8) + 2e-   [magnesium loses 2 electrons]
O (2,6) + 2e- -> O2- (2,8)         [oxygen gains 2 electrons]
Mg2+ + O2- -> MgO                  [held by electrostatic attraction]
Ions present: Mg2+ (magnesium cation) and O2- (oxide anion).

items.question: Explain why ionic compounds conduct electricity in the molten state but not in the solid state.
items.answer:
Ionic compounds require the movement of charged particles (ions) to conduct electricity.
IN SOLID STATE: In the solid state, the ions are arranged in a fixed rigid lattice structure. The electrostatic forces of attraction between the oppositely charged ions are very strong. The ions cannot move freely in this rigid structure. Since electricity requires movement of charged particles, ionic compounds do NOT conduct electricity in the solid state.
IN MOLTEN STATE: When ionic compounds are heated to their melting point, the rigid lattice structure breaks down. The ions become free to move. These mobile ions can carry electric charge and hence conduct electricity. The electrostatic forces are overcome by the heat supplied.
Similarly, ionic compounds dissolved in water also conduct electricity as the ions are free to move in the solution.

items.question: Explain with an example how sodium and chlorine combine to form sodium chloride. Draw a labelled diagram to show the electron transfer.
items.answer:
The combination of sodium and chlorine to form sodium chloride involves transfer of electrons:
SODIUM ATOM: Electronic configuration of Na is 2,8,1. It has 1 electron in its outermost shell. To attain noble gas configuration (like neon, 2,8), sodium needs to lose 1 electron:
Na (2,8,1) -> Na+ (2,8) + e-
Na+ is positively charged as it now has 11 protons but only 10 electrons.
CHLORINE ATOM: Electronic configuration of Cl is 2,8,7. It has 7 electrons in its outermost shell. To attain noble gas configuration (like argon, 2,8,8), chlorine needs to gain 1 electron:
Cl (2,8,7) + e- -> Cl- (2,8,8)
Cl- is negatively charged as it now has 17 protons but 18 electrons.
IONIC BOND: The positively charged Na+ and negatively charged Cl- attract each other with a strong electrostatic force to form sodium chloride (NaCl). NaCl does not exist as individual molecules but as aggregates of large numbers of Na+ and Cl- ions arranged in a regular lattice.

items.question: State four general properties of ionic compounds with brief explanations.
items.answer:
(i) PHYSICAL NATURE: Ionic compounds are solids at room temperature. They are somewhat hard due to the strong electrostatic forces of attraction between positive and negative ions. They are generally brittle and break into pieces when pressure is applied.
(ii) MELTING AND BOILING POINTS: Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points. This is because a large amount of energy is required to overcome the strong electrostatic inter-ionic attractions. For example, NaCl melts at 1074 K (Table 3.4).
(iii) SOLUBILITY: Ionic (electrovalent) compounds are generally soluble in water (a polar solvent) and insoluble in non-polar solvents like kerosene, petrol, etc.
(iv) CONDUCTION OF ELECTRICITY: Ionic compounds do not conduct electricity in the solid state (ions are in fixed positions in rigid lattice). However, they conduct electricity in the molten state or when dissolved in water, because ions become free to move and carry electric charge.

items.question: Compare the formation of NaCl and MgCl2, stating the number of electrons transferred, the ions formed, and the type of bonding.
items.answer:
FORMATION OF NaCl (Sodium Chloride):
- Na (atomic no. 11, configuration 2,8,1) has 1 electron in outermost shell.
- Na loses 1 electron: Na -> Na+ + e- (Na+ has configuration 2,8)
- Cl (atomic no. 17, configuration 2,8,7) has 7 electrons in outermost shell.
- Cl gains 1 electron: Cl + e- -> Cl- (Cl- has configuration 2,8,8)
- Ions formed: Na+ (sodium cation) and Cl- (chloride anion)
- Number of electrons transferred: 1 electron from Na to Cl.
- Bond: Na+ and Cl- are held by electrostatic force -> NaCl.
- Formula: NaCl (one Na+ and one Cl-)

FORMATION OF MgCl2 (Magnesium Chloride):
- Mg (atomic no. 12, configuration 2,8,2) has 2 electrons in outermost shell.
- Mg loses 2 electrons: Mg -> Mg2+ + 2e- (Mg2+ has configuration 2,8)
- Two Cl atoms each gain 1 electron: 2Cl + 2e- -> 2Cl- (each Cl- has 2,8,8)
- Ions formed: Mg2+ (magnesium cation) and 2 Cl- (chloride anions)
- Number of electrons transferred: 2 electrons (1 to each Cl).
- Bond: Mg2+ and 2Cl- held by electrostatic force -> MgCl2.
- Formula: MgCl2 (one Mg2+ and two Cl-)

COMPARISON:
- NaCl involves transfer of 1 electron; MgCl2 involves transfer of 2 electrons.
- Na forms +1 ion; Mg forms +2 ion.
- Both are ionic (electrovalent) compounds with high melting points and good electrical conductivity in solution.

items.question: What type of ions are formed when metals lose electrons?
items.explanation: When metals lose electrons, the number of protons (positive charges) becomes more than the number of electrons (negative charges). This results in a positively charged ion called a cation.

items.question: What is the electronic configuration of Na+ ion?
items.explanation: Sodium (Na) has electronic configuration 2, 8, 1. When it loses 1 electron to form Na+, the configuration becomes 2, 8 (same as neon, a noble gas). This stable configuration is why sodium easily forms Na+.

items.question: NaCl does not exist as molecules. It exists as:

options.A: Single atoms of Na and Cl

items.explanation: NaCl is an ionic compound. It does not exist as individual molecules of NaCl. Instead, it forms a crystal lattice structure consisting of large aggregates of oppositely charged Na+ and Cl- ions arranged regularly.

items.question: Why do ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points?

options.B: Because of strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions
options.C: Because they are insoluble in water
options.D: Because they have large molecular masses

items.explanation: In ionic compounds, positive and negative ions are held together by very strong electrostatic forces of attraction. A large amount of energy is needed to overcome these forces and separate the ions. This is why ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points (e.g., NaCl melts at 1074 K).

items.question: How many electrons does magnesium transfer when forming MgCl2?

options.B: 2 electrons both to one Cl atom
options.C: 1 electron to each of two Cl atoms (total 2 electrons)

items.explanation: Magnesium (Mg, config 2,8,2) loses 2 electrons to form Mg2+. These 2 electrons are transferred one each to two separate Cl atoms (each Cl gains 1 electron to form Cl-). Hence MgCl2 has one Mg2+ and two Cl-.

items.question: An ionic compound is dissolved in water. Which of the following statements is correct about its electrical conductivity?

options.A: It does not conduct because ions are in fixed positions
options.B: It conducts electricity because the free ions move
options.C: It does not conduct because it is a solid
options.D: It conducts because of free electrons

items.explanation: When an ionic compound dissolves in water, the ions separate (dissociate) and become free to move in the solution. These mobile ions can carry electric charge and hence ionic compounds conduct electricity in aqueous solution.

items.question: The valency of Ca is 2 and that of O is also 2. What is the formula of calcium oxide and how many electrons are transferred?
items.explanation: Ca has configuration 2,8,8,2. It loses 2 electrons to form Ca2+. Oxygen (config 2,6) gains 2 electrons to form O2-. One Ca2+ pairs with one O2- to form CaO. A total of 2 electrons are transferred from Ca to O.

items.question: Why do noble gases like neon and argon not form ionic compounds?

options.B: Noble gases have completely filled valence shells and do not need to gain or lose electrons

items.explanation: Noble gases (He, Ne, Ar etc.) have completely filled valence shells (He: 2; Ne: 2,8; Ar: 2,8,8). They have already attained stable configurations and therefore have no tendency to gain or lose electrons. Since ionic bond formation requires electron transfer, noble gases do not form ionic compounds.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: PHYSICAL NATURE: Ionic compounds are solids; somewhat hard due to strong inter-ionic forces; brittle (break when pressure applied).
MELTING AND BOILING POINTS: High melting and boiling points (Table 3.4):
NaCl: MP 1074 K, BP 1686 K
LiCl: MP 887 K, BP 1600 K
CaCl2: MP 1045 K, BP 1900 K
CaO: MP 2850 K, BP 3120 K
MgCl2: MP 981 K, BP 1685 K
SOLUBILITY: Generally soluble in water; insoluble in non-polar solvents (kerosene, petrol).
CONDUCTION OF ELECTRICITY:
In solid state: DO NOT conduct (ions are in fixed positions in rigid lattice; cannot move).
In molten state: DO conduct (heat overcomes electrostatic forces; ions become free to move).
In aqueous solution: DO conduct (dissolved ions are free to move).

sections.label: ACTIVITY 3.13:
sections.aim: To study the properties of ionic compounds.
sections.materials: Sodium chloride, potassium iodide, barium chloride or other salts; spatula; metal spatula; burner; beakers; petrol; kerosene; water; battery, bulb, switch, graphite rod electrodes (Fig. 3.7 and Fig. 3.8).
procedure: - Take samples of NaCl, KI, BaCl2 or any other salt from the science laboratory.
- Note the physical state of these salts (are they solids?).
- Heat a small amount of sample on a metal spatula directly on the flame (Fig. 3.7). Repeat with other samples.
- Observe: Did the samples melt? Did they impart colour to the flame?
- Try to dissolve the samples in water, petrol and kerosene. Are they soluble?
- Make a circuit as shown in Fig. 3.8 and insert the electrodes into a solution of one salt.
- Test the other salt samples too.
- Observe: Does the bulb glow? What is your inference about the nature of these compounds?
sections.observation: Ionic compounds are solids with high melting points. They do not melt easily when heated directly in a flame (some impart colour to flame). They dissolve in water but not in petrol or kerosene. The bulb glows when electrodes are inserted in the ionic solution (conducts electricity in solution).
sections.conclusion:
Ionic compounds are: (i) solids with high melting points, (ii) soluble in water but not in non-polar solvents, (iii) good conductors of electricity in aqueous solution.
